content: Kepone, also known as chlordecone, is a carcinogenic insecticide chemically related to mirex. It was used in the United States between 1966 and 1975, primarily in ant and roach baits. The substance was manufactured by the Allied Signal Company in Hopewell, Virginia. However, improper handling and disposal of Kepone led to significant environmental contamination, particularly in the James River, sparking a nationwide pollution controversy. Its use was officially banned in 1975. Kepone is a chlorinated polycyclic ketone insecticide and fungicide, with the chemical formula C10H2Cl10O. The substance, which exists as a dry powder, is readily absorbed through the skin and respiratory tract. Workers who were exposed to Kepone without adequate protection experienced a range of severe health effects. These included tremors, involuntary jerky eye movements (nystagmus), memory loss, headaches, slurred speech, unsteadiness, lack of coordination, weight loss, skin rashes, liver enlargement, decreased libido, sterility, chest pain, joint pain (arthralgia), and an increased risk of cancer. Kepone is highly persistent in the environment, with an estimated half-life of approximately 30 years. The long-term contamination of the James River had widespread consequences. In July 2005, an article in Richmond Magazine detailed the adverse health effects experienced by Allied Signal employees and highlighted how Dan Rather and CBS's 60 Minutes brought national attention to the Kepone crisis. The incident remains a notable example of industrial pollution and its consequences. The cultural impact of the Kepone crisis extended beyond environmental and health concerns. The punk band Dead Kennedys recorded a song titled Kepone Factory, which referenced the disaster and drew parallels to Minamata disease. The song was written in 1978 and performed live before being officially released on their 1981 album In God We Trust, Inc. Additionally, an indie rock band named Kepone, formed in Richmond, Virginia, in 1991, derived its name from the Kepone crisis. The band was originally a side project of Michael Bishop, a former bassist of GWAR.
